newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran delays return of German, Danish envoys.
newsitem.headline: Iran delays return of German, Danish envoys.

text.p: Iran on Wednesday raised the volume in its war of words with the European Union and ordered the German and Danish ambassadors to be kept out of the country for now.

Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati, speaking at a news conference in the Iranian capital, said Tehran "will not be upset if the German ambassador never returns to Tehran and we may even be...pleased", the official news agency IRNA said.
Velayati said in reply to a question about reports the Danish ambassador had delayed his return that the same applied to him, the Tehran daily Kayhan said.
Supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei also instructed the Foreign Ministry not to rush in sending diplomats back to the EU, Iran's largest trade partner.

EU countries except Greece withdrew their ambassadors from Tehran for consultations after a German court verdict that Iranian leaders ordered the 1992 assassination of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin. Iran has repeatedly denied being involved.
European foreign ministers on Tuesday announced they would allow the envoys' return but were suspending ministerial contacts with Iran.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani joined in the burst of bitter statements by Iran's top leadership, accusing the 15-nation EU of "childish games".
The latest blast from Tehran seemed certain to further strain already tense relations between EU capitals and the Islamic republic, bristling over the April 10 verdict.
Khamenei called Western states "unfair, ill-intentioned, shameless and brazen because of their baseless accusations against the Iranian nation and other nations of the world".

Gulf analysts said the statements from Tehran were the most acrimonious outburst against the EU since the 1989 row over Iranian death threats against British author Salman Rushdie whose novel "The Satanic Verses" was deemed blasphemous by Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.
But Khomeini's successor Khamenei, in a speech broadcast on Tehran radio, said Iran's arch-enemies the United States and Israel were responsible for the latest row.
"Of course, in my opinion, they (Europeans) have been deceived by the Zionists and the Americans. They have been pressured by the Americans," he said.
Khamenei also rejected any continued "critical dialogue" with the EU, which has suspended the policy aimed at keeping lines of communication with Iran open while seeking to change Iranian behaviour.
The five-year-old policy was championed by German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, who had also taken a lead in trying to persuade Iran to lift Khomeini's death edict on Rushdie.
Washington derided the EU policy as a total failure while pressing the bloc to take a tougher stand on Iran.

The United States welcomed news that "critical dialogue" was now dead, saying the EU shared the U.S. view "that Iran must respect the norms of international law, refrain from acts of terrorism and live up to international commitments on human rights and on proliferation issues".
But Rafsanjani, who is due to be replaced in an election on May 23, said Tehran itself had halted "critical dialogue" with Europe prior to the EU move.
"Critical dialogue, the suspension of which is being hailed as an achievement by Europeans, had been suspended before this at the instigation of Iran," he said in remarks quoted by IRNA.

"The Europeans have engaged in propaganda intrigues, indulged in stubborn and childish games, have become ashamed of themselves and have quickly put their hands up in the air; this is a sign of Iran's real strength," Rafsanjani said.
The total value of EU-Iran trade was $11.2 billion in 1995, the latest year for which figures are available.
